title: Voyager 1
summary: Launched to visit Jupiter and Saturn, it found volcanoes on another world, photographed the Earth as a tiny dot, and <mark>is now travelling between the stars, still sending data home.</mark>

chapters.title: A once-in-175-years chance
chapters.summary: Engineers noticed something rare.
chapters.body:
Engineers noticed something rare. In the late 1970s Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune would all be on the same side of the Sun, in an arc. That alignment comes around about once every 175 years.

A spacecraft could swing around one planet and steal a little of its speed to reach the next. This gravity assist cut a trip to Neptune from thirty years to about twelve.

A plan to visit all four was too expensive, so in 1972 NASA approved two spacecraft for Jupiter and Saturn. Quietly, the engineers built them to last much longer.

media.title: Note
media.text:
Gravity assist:
Neptune in 12 years instead of 30.

chapters.title: Borrowing speed
chapters.summary: In 1961 a student working at JPL, Michael Minovitch, used the laboratory's computers to show something surprising: a spacecraft flying close behind a planet can steal a little of the planet's speed around the Sun.
chapters.body:
In 1961 a student working at JPL, Michael Minovitch, used the laboratory's computers to show something surprising: a spacecraft flying close behind a planet can steal a little of the planet's speed around the Sun.

The planet slows down by an amount far too small to measure. The spacecraft is flung onwards much faster, without burning any fuel. This trick is called a gravity assist.

In 1965 another young engineer, Gary Flandro, noticed that in the late 1970s the four giant planets would line up so that one spacecraft could bounce from each to the next.
chapters.marginNote: Free speed, stolen from a planet.

media.title: Gary Flandro
media.caption: Gary Flandro, who found the rare line-up of the outer planets in 1965, photographed in 2017.

chapters.title: Pioneers went first
chapters.summary: Before the Voyagers, two smaller NASA probes scouted the way.
chapters.body:
Before the Voyagers, two smaller NASA probes scouted the way. Pioneer 10, launched in March 1972, was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and, in December 1973, to fly past Jupiter.

It found Jupiter's radiation far stronger than expected, strong enough to damage electronics. The Voyagers were redesigned with extra shielding because of it. Pioneer 11 followed, flying past Jupiter and then, in 1979, Saturn.

Each Pioneer carried a metal plaque with a drawing of a man and a woman and a map showing where the Earth is.

media.title: A Pioneer on its way
media.caption: A painting of a Pioneer spacecraft heading out of the Solar System.

media.title: The Pioneer plaque
media.caption: The plaque carried by Pioneer 10 and 11, designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake.

chapters.title: From Mariner to Voyager
chapters.summary: The project was approved in 1972 under a plain name: Mariner Jupiter-Saturn 1977, after the family of Mariner probes that JPL had sent to Mars, Venus and Mercury.
chapters.body:
The project was approved in 1972 under a plain name: Mariner Jupiter-Saturn 1977, after the family of Mariner probes that JPL had sent to Mars, Venus and Mercury.

The spacecraft grew into something much bigger than a Mariner. In March 1977, a few months before launch, NASA gave the mission a new name: Voyager.

Officially the twins were only going to Jupiter and Saturn. Their builders made them strong enough to go much further.

media.title: Mariner Jupiter-Saturn
media.caption: A 1975 painting of the spacecraft, from when it was still called Mariner Jupiter-Saturn 1977.

chapters.title: The spacecraft
chapters.summary: Each Voyager is about the size of a small car, about 825 kilograms.
chapters.body:
Each Voyager is about the size of a small car, about 825 kilograms. A white dish 3.7 metres across always points back at the Earth. Below it a ten-sided box holds the computers, the radio and fuel for small thrusters.

Solar panels would be useless so far from the Sun. Instead three nuclear batteries turn the heat of decaying plutonium into electricity: about 470 watts at launch, a few watts less every year.

Its computers have less memory than a simple modern calculator. They are still running.
chapters.marginNote: No solar panels. Plutonium heat instead.

media.title: Voyager, part by part
media.caption: The structure of the Voyager spacecraft and its instruments.

chapters.title: Power from plutonium
chapters.summary: At Jupiter the Sun gives only a twenty-fifth of the light it gives at the Earth.
chapters.body:
At Jupiter the Sun gives only a twenty-fifth of the light it gives at the Earth. Further out, solar panels would be useless.

So each Voyager carries three radioisotope thermoelectric generators on a long arm. Inside, balls of plutonium oxide stay hot as they slowly decay. Rows of thermocouples turn that heat straight into electricity, with no moving parts.

The plutonium loses half its power every 88 years, and the thermocouples wear out, so the power drops a little every year.
chapters.marginNote: Heat into electricity, for half a century.

media.title: A generator
media.caption: One of Voyager's radioisotope thermoelectric generators, cut open.

chapters.title: Built to last
chapters.summary: Nobody could fix a Voyager once it left.
chapters.body:
Nobody could fix a Voyager once it left. So everything important was built in pairs, and the spacecraft was given the ability to look after itself.

If something failed, its computers could switch to a backup and wait safely for instructions. Every part was shaken, heated, frozen and blasted with radiation before launch.

The mission was planned to last about five years. It has lasted almost fifty.
chapters.marginNote: Planned for five years. Still going.

media.title: Shaken before launch
media.caption: A Voyager spacecraft during vibration testing at JPL.

chapters.title: The instruments
chapters.summary: Voyager carries about ten scientific instruments.
chapters.body:
Voyager carries about ten scientific instruments. Some measure magnetic fields, charged particles and radio waves around it. Others look at things far away.

The cameras and the instruments that study light sit on a scan platform at the end of a boom. It turns to point them at a planet or a moon while the rest of the spacecraft keeps its dish aimed at the Earth.

Each Voyager has two cameras: a wide-angle one and a narrow-angle one, like a zoom lens.

media.title: The scan platform
media.caption: Voyager's scan platform, carrying the cameras and other instruments that look at planets.

chapters.title: A message in a bottle
chapters.summary: Both Voyagers will leave the Solar System, so a committee led by Carl Sagan chose a message for anyone who might find one: a gold-plated copper record with instructions engraved on the cover.
chapters.body:
Both Voyagers will leave the Solar System, so a committee led by Carl Sagan chose a message for anyone who might find one: a gold-plated copper record with instructions engraved on the cover.

It holds greetings in 55 languages, sounds of the Earth, music from Bach to Chuck Berry, and 116 pictures encoded as sound. The cover shows how to play it and where the Earth is, using pulsars as a map.

Voyager 1 will not come close to another star for about 40 000 years. The record is a picture of humanity in 1977, sent out on purpose.
chapters.marginNote: 55 languages. 116 pictures. A map made of pulsars.

media.title: The Golden Record
media.caption: The cover of the Golden Record, with engraved instructions for playing it and finding the Earth.

chapters.title: What is on the record
chapters.summary: The committee had only a few months to choose what should speak for the whole Earth.
chapters.body:
The committee had only a few months to choose what should speak for the whole Earth. They settled on greetings, sounds, music and pictures.

The greetings are in 55 languages, from Akkadian, spoken five thousand years ago, to Wu, a dialect of modern Chinese. The sounds include wind, thunder, birds, whales, a kiss, footsteps, laughter and a mother with her baby. The music runs for about ninety minutes: Bach, Beethoven and Stravinsky, Chuck Berry's Johnny B. Goode, Navajo night chant, a Peruvian wedding song, Indian raga and Georgian choir.

The 116 pictures, stored as sound, show the human body, families, cities, food and the planets.
chapters.marginNote: A kiss, a heartbeat, Johnny B. Goode.

media.title: The Golden Record
media.caption: A copy of the Golden Record. The cover shows how to play it.

chapters.title: Voyager 2 goes first
chapters.summary: The twins were numbered by the order in which they would reach Jupiter, not the order of launch.
chapters.body:
The twins were numbered by the order in which they would reach Jupiter, not the order of launch. Voyager 2 went first, on 20 August 1977, on a slower path that kept the way open to Uranus and Neptune.

Its first days were worrying. The shaking of launch confused its computer, which kept switching between backup systems, and one boom seemed not to have locked open.

The engineers sorted it out. Two weeks later its twin was ready.

media.title: Voyager 2 lifts off
media.caption: A Titan IIIE-Centaur launches Voyager 2 on 20 August 1977.

chapters.title: Launch
chapters.summary: Voyager 2 left first, on 20 August 1977.
chapters.body:
Voyager 2 left first, on 20 August 1977. Voyager 1 followed on 5 September, on a faster path, and by December it had overtaken its twin.

On 18 September 1977 it turned back and took the first picture of the Earth and the Moon together, two crescents in the dark.
chapters.marginNote: Second to leave, first to arrive.

media.title: Titan IIIE
media.caption: The Titan IIIE rocket with Voyager 1, Cape Canaveral.

media.title: Earth and Moon together
media.caption: The first picture of the Earth and the Moon in one frame, 18 September 1977.

media.title: Voyager 1 launches
media.caption: Film of the launch of Voyager 1 on a Titan IIIE rocket, 5 September 1977.

chapters.title: Close to empty
chapters.summary: Voyager 1's launch looked perfect from the ground.
chapters.body:
Voyager 1's launch looked perfect from the ground. In fact the second stage of the Titan rocket shut down early, leaving the spacecraft short of speed.

The Centaur upper stage noticed and burned longer to make up the difference. When it finally shut down, it had only about three and a half seconds of fuel left.

It was the closest call of the whole mission, and it was over in a few minutes, long before anyone on the ground understood it.
chapters.marginNote: Three and a half seconds of fuel.

media.title: Voyager 1 lifts off
media.caption: The launch of Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977.

chapters.title: Jupiter
chapters.summary: Voyager 1 passed closest to Jupiter on 5 March 1979.
chapters.body:
Voyager 1 passed closest to Jupiter on 5 March 1979. Its pictures showed the storms in astonishing detail, including the Great Red Spot, a storm bigger than the Earth.

On 9 March the engineer Linda Morabito noticed a strange bright crescent at the edge of the moon Io. It was a plume from a volcano, rising hundreds of kilometres. Io turned out to be the most volcanic place in the Solar System: the first active volcanoes seen anywhere except the Earth.

media.title: The Great Red Spot
media.caption: Jupiter's Great Red Spot from Voyager 1.
media.credit: NASA, JPL, Björn Jónsson. Public domain.

media.title: A volcano on Io
media.caption: The plume of the volcano Loki at the edge of Io.
media.text: Io, a plume at the edge

media.title: Note
media.text:
9 March 1979:
Linda Morabito spots the plume.

chapters.title: Volcanoes on Io
chapters.summary: Just days before Voyager 1 reached Jupiter, three scientists published a prediction: Jupiter's pull squeezes the moon Io back and forth so strongly that its inside must be melting.
chapters.body:
Just days before Voyager 1 reached Jupiter, three scientists published a prediction: Jupiter's pull squeezes the moon Io back and forth so strongly that its inside must be melting. There might be volcanoes.

They were right. Voyager 1 found nine erupting volcanoes on Io, throwing sulphur hundreds of kilometres into space. Its surface, yellow, orange and black, is the youngest in the Solar System, covered again and again by lava.

It was the first time active volcanoes had been seen anywhere except the Earth.

media.title: Io over Jupiter
media.caption: Io passing in front of Jupiter, from Voyager 1 pictures of 1979.
media.credit: NASA, processed by Andrea Luck. CC BY 2.0

chapters.title: A ring around Jupiter
chapters.summary: Saturn's rings had been known for centuries.
chapters.body:
Saturn's rings had been known for centuries. Most scientists did not expect Jupiter to have any.

Voyager 1 took a long-exposure picture just in case, as it crossed the plane where a ring would be. It found a faint, thin ring of dust.

Voyager 2 photographed it more clearly a few months later. We now know that all four giant planets have rings.

media.title: Jupiter's ring
media.caption: Jupiter's faint ring, photographed by Voyager 2 in 1979.

media.title: Note
media.text:
Saturn: rings.
Jupiter: rings.
Uranus, Neptune: rings.

chapters.title: The four big moons
chapters.summary: Galileo found Jupiter's four largest moons in 1610.
chapters.body:
Galileo found Jupiter's four largest moons in 1610. For more than 360 years they were just points of light. Voyager turned them into worlds.

Io had volcanoes. Europa was smooth ice covered in long cracks, perhaps floating on a hidden ocean. Ganymede, the biggest moon in the Solar System, is larger than the planet Mercury. Callisto is battered by craters all over.

Europa's ocean is now one of the best places to look for life beyond the Earth.
chapters.marginNote: Four points of light, four worlds.

media.title: Jupiter with Io and Europa
media.caption: Jupiter with its moons Io and Europa in front of it, photographed by Voyager 1.
media.credit: NASA / JPL / Björn Jónsson. Public domain.

media.title: Ganymede
media.caption: Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System, seen by Voyager 1.

chapters.title: Saturn and Titan
chapters.summary: At Saturn, Voyager 1 showed that the rings are thousands of narrow ringlets, with dark "spokes" that come and go and thin rings kept in shape by tiny moons.
chapters.body:
At Saturn, Voyager 1 showed that the rings are thousands of narrow ringlets, with dark "spokes" that come and go and thin rings kept in shape by tiny moons.

To pass close to Titan, the only moon with a thick atmosphere, it had to take a path out of the plane of the planets, and could never reach Uranus or Neptune. The scientists chose Titan. It found air thicker than the Earth's, wrapped in an orange haze.

Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 1 headed out of the Solar System.
chapters.marginNote: Titan, or Uranus and Neptune. They chose Titan.

media.title: Saturn, looking back
media.caption: A crescent Saturn, seen by Voyager 1 as it left.

media.title: The rings
media.caption: Saturn's rings, made of thousands of narrow ringlets.

media.title: Voyager 1 at Saturn
media.caption: A JPL film from November 1980 about Voyager 1's flight past Saturn.

chapters.title: Spokes and shepherds
chapters.summary: Close up, Saturn's rings were stranger than anyone had imagined.
chapters.body:
Close up, Saturn's rings were stranger than anyone had imagined. Dark streaks, called spokes, stretched across them, came and went, and turned with the planet instead of with the rings.

The thin outer F ring looked twisted and braided. Voyager 1 found two small moons, Prometheus and Pandora, one on each side of it, whose gravity keeps the ring narrow. They are called shepherd moons.

The spokes are thought to be fine dust lifted above the rings by electric charges. They are still not fully understood.

media.title: Saturn's rings
media.caption: Saturn's rings close up, photographed by Voyager 2.

rows: dark streaks that come and go

chapters.title: Voyager 2 goes on
chapters.summary: Because Voyager 1 chose Titan, only its twin could continue the Grand Tour.
chapters.body:
Because Voyager 1 chose Titan, only its twin could continue the Grand Tour. Voyager 2 passed Jupiter and Saturn and then flew on to Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989.

It found new moons and faint rings at both. At Neptune it saw a dark storm the size of the Earth and, on the moon Triton, geysers of dark material. It is still the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune.

In November 2018 Voyager 2 also crossed into interstellar space.

media.title: Neptune
media.caption: Neptune photographed by Voyager 2 in August 1989, with its Great Dark Spot.

chapters.tabLabel: Why it nearly did not happen
chapters.title: Why it nearly did not happen
chapters.summary: After Saturn, Carl Sagan began asking for one more picture: turn the cameras back and photograph the whole family of planets from outside.
chapters.body:
After Saturn, Carl Sagan began asking for one more picture: turn the cameras back and photograph the whole family of planets from outside.

Many on the team said no. The pictures would have little scientific value, and pointing the cameras close to the Sun could damage them. Engineers needed time and money to plan it.

Sagan kept asking for years. In 1989 NASA's new head, Richard Truly, approved it. By then Voyager 1 was far beyond Neptune.

media.title: Close to the Sun
media.caption: Part of the family portrait near the Sun, with the Earth and Venus. The bright glare is why many feared for the cameras.

chapters.title: The family portrait
chapters.place: About six billion kilometres from the Sun
chapters.summary: The pale blue dot is one frame of a larger picture.
chapters.body:
The pale blue dot is one frame of a larger picture. Voyager 1 took sixty images in a sweep across the sky to make a family portrait of the Solar System, seen from outside.

Six planets appear: Venus, the Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Three are missing. Mercury was too close to the glare of the Sun, Mars was lost in scattered light, and Pluto was too small and dark.

They were the last pictures Voyager 1 ever took. Its cameras were switched off to save power for the long journey ahead.
chapters.marginNote: The last pictures it ever took.

media.title: The family portrait
media.caption: The mosaic of the Solar System taken by Voyager 1 on 14 February 1990.

media.title: Where the planets were
media.caption: Where each planet appeared in the sixty frames.

chapters.title: A pale blue dot
chapters.place: About six billion kilometres from the Sun
chapters.summary: Carl Sagan had argued for one more picture: turn around and photograph the planets from the outside.
chapters.body:
Carl Sagan had argued for one more picture: turn around and photograph the planets from the outside. On 14 February 1990 Voyager 1 took sixty pictures. Then its cameras were switched off for good.

In one frame the Earth is a single tiny dot, less than a pixel, caught in a beam of sunlight. Sagan called it the pale blue dot: every person who ever lived, lived there.
chapters.marginNote: Less than a pixel. Everyone, ever.

media.title: The Pale Blue Dot
media.caption: The Earth, the speck inside the band of light, from about six billion kilometres.

media.title: Quote
media.text: Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us.
media.author: Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot

chapters.title: The edge of the bubble
chapters.place: About 94 times the Earth's distance from the Sun
chapters.summary: The solar wind blows outward at hundreds of kilometres per second.
chapters.body:
The solar wind blows outward at hundreds of kilometres per second. Far out, it meets the thin gas between the stars and has to slow down.

Where it suddenly drops below the speed of sound, there is a kind of shock wave, called the termination shock. Voyager 1 crossed it in December 2004, about 94 times further from the Sun than the Earth.

Beyond it lies the heliosheath, a slow, turbulent zone between the solar wind and interstellar space.

media.title: The Voyagers in the heliosheath
media.caption: An illustration of the two Voyagers in the heliosheath, the outer layer of the Sun's bubble.

chapters.title: Into interstellar space
chapters.summary: In 1998 Voyager 1 became the most distant human-made object.
chapters.body:
In 1998 Voyager 1 became the most distant human-made object. On 25 August 2012 it left the bubble of the solar wind and entered interstellar space, the first spacecraft ever to do so.

Its radio is about as powerful as a refrigerator light. In late 2026 it is close to one light-day away: a command takes almost a full day to arrive.

In 2023 it started sending nonsense. The team traced it to one broken memory chip and, in 2024, moved the code by radio from 24 billion kilometres away. It worked.
chapters.marginNote: Play the tape: interstellar space, turned into sound.

media.title: Note
media.text:
One broken chip.
Fixed by radio from 24 billion km.

media.title: The edge of the Sun's bubble
media.caption: An illustration of the bubble the Sun blows around itself, and Voyager 1 crossing its edge.

chapters.title: Listening to space
chapters.summary: How do you know when you have left the Sun's bubble?
chapters.body:
How do you know when you have left the Sun's bubble? Voyager 1's instrument for measuring the density of the gas had stopped working long ago.

The answer came from the Sun itself. In 2012 a blast from the Sun reached the spacecraft and made the gas around it vibrate. Voyager's plasma wave instrument picked up the vibration, and its pitch showed that the gas was about forty times denser than inside the bubble.

That density could only belong to interstellar space. NASA turned the measurement into sound. It is on the tape by the radio.

media.title: Note
media.text:
Play the tape by the radio:
the sound of interstellar gas.

chapters.title: Talking across the dark
chapters.summary: Voyager 1 talks to the Earth through the Deep Space Network: three groups of giant dishes in California, Spain and Australia, spread around the globe so that one of them can always see the spacecraft.
chapters.body:
Voyager 1 talks to the Earth through the Deep Space Network: three groups of giant dishes in California, Spain and Australia, spread around the globe so that one of them can always see the spacecraft.

Its transmitter has only about 23 watts. By the time the signal reaches the Earth it is unimaginably faint, and only the largest dishes, 70 metres across, can still hear it. The data arrives at about 160 bits per second, slower than the oldest dial-up modem.

Every command sent to it takes almost a day to arrive, and the answer takes another day to come back.

media.title: The dishes at Canberra
media.caption: The Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex in Australia, one of the three stations of the Deep Space Network.

chapters.title: A broken chip
chapters.summary: In November 2023 Voyager 1 stopped sending readable data.
chapters.body:
In November 2023 Voyager 1 stopped sending readable data. Its signal still arrived, but it carried nonsense.

The team worked out that one memory chip in a computer had failed, taking with it part of the software. Nobody could replace it. So they split the code into pieces and moved them, one by one, into other parts of the memory, by radio.

Each test took almost two days for the command to arrive and the answer to come back. By June 2024 all the instruments were sending science again.

media.title: The dish at Goldstone
media.caption: The 70-metre dish at Goldstone, California, one of the antennas used to talk to Voyager 1.

chapters.title: The last years
chapters.summary: Voyager 1's nuclear batteries lose a few watts every year.
chapters.body:
Voyager 1's nuclear batteries lose a few watts every year. To keep it going, the team has been switching off heaters and instruments one at a time, deciding each year what it can live without.

Some time in the 2030s there will not be enough power to run any instrument, and then not even the radio. When Voyager 1 falls silent it will not stop. It will keep moving at about 17 kilometres per second, with nothing to slow it down.

In about 40 000 years it will pass within about 1.6 light-years of a faint star called Gliese 445. It will still be carrying the Golden Record.

media.title: The Voyager team
media.caption: Ed Stone, the mission's chief scientist, at a press conference in 1990.

chapters.title: One light-day
chapters.place: About 26 billion kilometres from the Earth
chapters.summary: Light from the Sun reaches the Earth in about eight minutes.
chapters.body:
Light from the Sun reaches the Earth in about eight minutes. Light from Voyager 1 now takes a whole day.

In November 2026 Voyager 1 is about 26 billion kilometres away, the distance light travels in 24 hours. It is the first object made by people to be one light-day from home.

Even so, the nearest star is still more than four light-years away. Voyager 1 has barely started.
chapters.marginNote: A day for light. Four years to the next star.

media.title: Where the Voyagers are
media.caption: A NASA chart of the two Voyagers and the Sun's bubble.

chapters.title: Why it never stops
chapters.summary: Voyager 1 has not fired its main engines for almost fifty years.
chapters.body:
Voyager 1 has not fired its main engines for almost fifty years. It does not need fuel to keep going. It would need fuel to stop.

Out between the stars there is almost nothing to slow it down. Newton's first law says a moving object keeps its speed and direction until a force changes them.

On the monitor: push a box on a field with no friction, and watch it keep going.
